prompt.context:
Our client Mallgreens is a large pharma retail company. It wants to acquire a smaller pharmacy retailer, BrightAid. The operational footprint of the two companies looks like this:

| Company    | States | Stores | Employees |
|------------|--------|--------|-----------|
| Mallgreens | 50     | 5,000  | 2,000     |
| BrightAid  | 13 (Coasts) | 2,000 | 1,000 |
prompt.question: Mallgreens wants us to assess this acquisition and understand potential risks.

clarifying_info.q: What services does each company provide?
clarifying_info.a: Mallgreens provides pharmacy, clinical, photography, and convenience store services. BrightAid provides pharmacy and clinical services only.

clarifying_info.q: Do the two companies have similar operating models?
clarifying_info.a: No. The two companies have very different distribution models.

exhibits.title: Store Footprint by State
exhibits.shows: A table listing selected states with the number of stores each company operates in that state.
exhibits.data: CA: Mallgreens 400, BrightAid 250; WA: Mallgreens 280, BrightAid 65; NY: Mallgreens 350, BrightAid 200; MI: Mallgreens 280, BrightAid 0; IN: Mallgreens 220, BrightAid 0; TX: Mallgreens 350, BrightAid 180

exhibits.title: California Store Summary by Distance and Profitability
exhibits.shows: A table summarizing California stores segmented by distance from the nearest Mallgreens/BrightAid store and by profit/loss status.
exhibits.data: <0.5 mile: 200 profit-making, 100 loss-making; 0.5–2 miles: 80 profit-making, 60 loss-making; >2 miles: 70 profit-making, 40 loss-making

framework: 1. Synergies — Revenue: expanded selling power, new locations for photography and convenience services; Cost: increased buying power with manufacturers, retail footprint consolidation, corporate/executive function consolidation

2. Acquisition & Integration Costs — People: lock-in bonuses for retained employees, severance packages for exited employees; Operational: IT integration, marketing/rebranding; Long-term: capital gains tax
3. Risks — FTC antitrust concern if combined market share is too high; customer, vendor, and competitor response

questions.prompt: In which states will you consolidate stores, and why? (Exhibit 1)
questions.guidance: Focus on states where BOTH companies have meaningful presence — that is where overlap creates consolidation opportunity. States where only Mallgreens operates (MI, IN) offer no BrightAid overlap and thus no near-term consolidation. States where both companies have large footprints (CA, NY, TX) are the priority targets. WA has overlap but BrightAid's presence is relatively small. Key factors driving consolidation: proximity of stores to each other, redundancy in coverage, and cost of maintaining duplicate locations.

questions.prompt: Which California stores do you recommend closing, and what do you recommend for the remaining loss-making stores? (Exhibit 2)
questions.guidance: Use a tiered framework based on proximity and profitability. Close all loss-making stores within 0.5 miles of another store — customers can easily transfer to a nearby location, so there is minimal revenue risk and immediate cost savings (100 stores). For loss-making stores 0.5–2 miles away (60 stores): survey customers on brand stickiness and willingness to travel; assess whether short-to-mid-term transformation measures can turn them profitable. For loss-making stores >2 miles away (40 stores): these serve as anchor footprint locations; invest in long-term profitability transformation rather than closing, because retail presence at scale requires some loss-making outposts.

questions.prompt: What key questions can market regulators raise, and how do you ensure the deal and combined entity comply with legal requirements?
questions.guidance:
The FTC's primary concern is whether the combined entity's market share exceeds allowable thresholds. The answer differs depending on deal structure:

Stock purchase: acquirer buys all or partial stock; all assets, liabilities, and contracts transfer. More complex — Mallgreens would likely need to commit to divestitures post-close (e.g., sell its photography and convenience store business) to bring combined pharmacy market share below FTC thresholds.

Asset purchase: only selected assets are purchased; contracts and liabilities do not transfer. Mallgreens can selectively buy only certain BrightAid stores to remain within FTC thresholds from the outset, giving more flexibility to avoid regulatory issues pre-close.

brainstorming.prompt: Brainstorm the mechanics of the acquisition across three dimensions: (1) distribution model differences and how switching models could reduce costs, (2) whether cross/up-selling opportunities exist given both companies offer the same core pharmaceutical and clinical services in a saturated market, and (3) the pros and cons of a stock purchase vs. asset purchase in this specific deal.

categories.name: Distribution model cost reduction
ideas: Adopt the lower-cost distribution model for the combined entity
Consolidate warehousing and logistics under one network
Renegotiate supplier contracts from a position of greater volume
Eliminate redundant distribution centers in overlapping geographies

categories.name: Cross/up-selling opportunities
ideas: BrightAid stores on the coasts can add Mallgreens' photography and convenience services, creating new revenue streams in those markets
Expanded clinical services (e.g., flu shots, health screenings) across a larger combined store network
Loyalty program cross-pollination to capture BrightAid customers into Mallgreens ecosystem
Private label products sold across expanded store count

categories.name: Stock purchase vs. asset purchase
ideas: Stock purchase pros: faster, all contracts and relationships transfer, simpler operationally post-close
Stock purchase cons: all liabilities transfer including litigation risk; likely requires FTC-mandated divestitures; harder to cherry-pick only desirable assets
Asset purchase pros: can select only the best BrightAid stores; avoid inheriting liabilities; easier to stay below FTC thresholds
Asset purchase cons: slower and more complex transaction; must renegotiate contracts individually; may lose some key vendor/customer relationships that do not transfer automatically

recommendation: Mallgreens should proceed with the acquisition of BrightAid
Close 100 loss-making stores within 0.5 miles of other Mallgreens stores immediately
Survey customers of the 60 loss-making stores within 0.5–2 miles to assess brand stickiness and determine retention vs. closure
Invest in long-term profitability transformation for the 40 loss-making stores more than 2 miles from another store
risks: Potential FTC concern over combined market share of the resulting pharmacy retail entity
Competitor and supplier response to the newly enlarged entity
Integration execution risk — especially IT, distribution, and workforce
next_steps: Begin integration planning with focus on systems, procurement, and distribution
Define a communication plan for customers and employees to manage transition uncertainty
Evaluate deal structure (stock vs. asset purchase) in consultation with legal and regulatory advisors to determine the approach that keeps the deal within FTC thresholds
